This example revisits the empirical application in
[Sant’Anna and Xu (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2025.106147), using
`np` to estimate both generalized propensity scores and outcome regressions.
The same data and analogous package functions give results in broad agreement
with the authors’ findings. It is a replication/reproduction hybrid: a
same-data robustness check with independently estimated nuisance functions
and bandwidths.

[Download the complete R script](www/np_npRmpi/difference_in_differences/np_composition_did.R).
It reads pinned public data into memory, freshly fits both nuisance stages,
and prints the outcome table below. It requires `np` 0.80-1 or later and
internet access; it does not install packages or create folders or output
files. Allow a few minutes for bandwidth selection and leave-one-out fits.
Progress messages identify the current stage.

## The application and target

The application studies whether tariff reductions reduced bribery on shipments
entering Mozambique. Treatment identifies products whose tariffs fell in 2008;
the data contain shipments observed before and after the change. The four
outcomes describe whether a bribe was paid, its logged amount, and logged
bribe-to-value and bribe-to-tonnage ratios.

The target is the average treatment effect for treated shipments in the
post-treatment population. Conditional parallel trends, no anticipation and
appropriate overlap provide the identifying assumptions. With repeated
cross-sections, the observed covariate distribution can change across periods.
The composition-robust estimator allows for that change when constructing the
comparison for treated post-treatment observations.

The script preserves the authors’ preprocessing, adjustment variables and
common complete-case sample. There are **1,084 observations**: 120 treated/post,
56 treated/pre, 824 control/post and 84 control/pre. Each outcome uses two
continuous predictors and nine unordered predictors. The first two outcomes
share the same predictor design and therefore share their propensity fit.

## Estimating the nuisance functions with np

The implementation uses the four treatment/time cells as the response classes
for `npconmode`. Their conditional probabilities supply the generalized
propensity scores. Separate local-linear outcome regressions describe the
conditional mean in each cell. The script combines these predictions through
the normalized composition-robust ATT score, coded explicitly in R.

::: {.gallery-scroll-table}
| Component | Authors’ implementation | This np example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propensities | Local multinomial-logit likelihood | Local-constant conditional class probabilities from `npconmode` |
| Propensity bandwidths | Shared continuous and unordered bandwidths | Separate predictor and class-response bandwidths from `npcdensbw`, selected by likelihood cross-validation |
| Outcome regressions | Local-linear fits with shared bandwidths | Local-linear `npreg` fits with the same two-parameter sharing structure, freshly selected by pooled leave-one-out squared error |
| Continuous kernel | Epanechnikov | Gaussian |
:::

These adaptations use available `np` functions to perform comparable tasks.
Gaussian kernels and separate propensity bandwidths are choices for this
specification; the package also supports Epanechnikov kernels. Unordered
predictors use Li–Racine kernels, and the class response uses normalized
Aitchison–Aitken smoothing. The shared outcome-bandwidth search is a small
R `optim` wrapper around public `np` functions.

Own-observation predictions are leave-one-out, holding the selected bandwidths
fixed. Counterfactual outcomes for treated post-treatment observations use the
other cells’ fitted regressions. Following the archived application, estimated
probabilities are clipped to [0.01, 0.99] without subsequent renormalization;
raw probabilities remain available for inspection. This example follows the
application’s leave-one-out construction. The separate
[Doubly Robust Treatment Effects](doubly_robust_cate.qmd) example illustrates
fold-based cross-fitting for a different target and design.

## Outcome comparison

The table reports composition-robust ATT estimates, with clustered standard
errors in parentheses. The published column contains the corresponding Table 4
results at the precision retained in the authors’ archive. Every `np` entry
uses freshly estimated propensities, outcome means and bandwidths.

::: {.gallery-scroll-table}
| Outcome | Sant’Anna–Xu | np robustness check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bribe probability | -0.3068 (0.1086) | -0.2853 (0.1372) |
| Log(1 + bribe) | -2.8884 (0.9148) | -2.4308 (1.6439) |
| Log(1 + bribe / shipment value) | -0.0274 (0.0145) | -0.0060 (0.0039) |
| Log(1 + bribe / shipment tonnage) | -1.1307 (0.6346) | -0.8354 (1.1510) |
:::

All four effect directions agree. The estimated reduction in bribe probability
is about **28.5 percentage points**, compared with **30.7** in the published
results. Three point estimates differ by at most about half of the corresponding
published clustered standard error. The shipment-value effect is substantially
smaller, and log bribes no longer meet the conventional 5% significance
threshold. Bribe probability remains significant at 5%; both ratio outcomes
have normal 95% intervals containing zero in both implementations.

The script implements clustered multiplier inference explicitly: 9,999 Mammen
draws, seed 1234, and an interquartile-range scale estimate. It holds nuisance
fits and bandwidths fixed and clusters by four-digit product code. There are
131 clusters, with the largest containing 550 observations. These uncertainty
calculations are part of the supplied script; ordinary regression `se()` values
are not used as ATT standard errors.

## Reproduce and inspect the results

Download the script, then run:

```r
source("np_composition_did.R")
did_results$table       # Formatted published/np comparison
did_results$comparison  # Numerical estimates, SEs and normal 95% np intervals
```

`did_results` also contains the analysis data, raw propensity estimates,
selected bandwidths, outcome predictions, score contributions and session
information. The published constants enter only after fitting. The script
uses no saved nuisance fits and has no dependency on the authors’ package.

The Gaussian specification was selected for illustration after a bounded
comparison of estimators and kernels. The
[reproducibility and sensitivity note](www/np_npRmpi/difference_in_differences/README.md)
records those alternatives, including incomplete Epanechnikov fits, numerical
checks and source provenance. This supports the reported robustness comparison;
it does not establish identical inference for every specification.

Download the [numerical outcome table](www/np_npRmpi/difference_in_differences/comparison.csv)
or [standalone verification results](www/np_npRmpi/difference_in_differences/standalone_parity.csv).
For regression discontinuity and a randomized-trial example, see
[Causal Inference with Local Polynomials](causal_inference.qmd).

## Reference and scope

The reference is Sant’Anna, P. H. C. and Xu, Q. (2026),
“Difference-in-Differences with compositional changes,” *Journal of Econometrics*,
253, 106147. See the [published paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2025.106147)
and [open manuscript](https://psantanna.com/files/DiD_CC.pdf).
